objection

/ub-JEK-shun/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Objection means a statement of disagreement or disapproval that a person raises or lodges, especially in a formal setting.

The defense lawyer rose with an objection the moment the witness began describing rumors instead of facts.

Example

When the city posted notice of a proposed four-story warehouse, Mr. Okafor filed a formal objection, arguing that the building's loading docks would send delivery trucks down his quiet street at all hours.

Mr. Okafor made one specific, formal statement of opposition and submitted it through an official process, which is exactly what an objection is. Notice that it targets a single proposal for a stated reason rather than expressing general disagreement.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

protest: A protest is a public show of opposition, often an organized event with crowds, marches, and chanting; it happens out loud and in the open. An objection is a statement: one specific point of disagreement raised or filed, sometimes quietly, by a single person.

complaint: A complaint is a statement of dissatisfaction: something is wrong and you want it noted or fixed, from cold soup to an unfair fee. It looks backward at a grievance. An objection pushes back against a proposal or decision before it stands.

challenge: A challenge questions whether something is valid at all, the way a court challenge asks judges to strike a law down; it attacks legitimacy. An objection is narrower: it registers disagreement with one particular point or step, without denying anyone's right to decide.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

approval: a favorable opinion of something

endorsement: public support for something

Where it sits · how forcefully disagreement is voiced

concern → objection → outcry

concern vs. objection: A concern is milder; voicing a concern raises a worry gently, while an objection states opposition directly.

outcry vs. objection: An objection is stronger than a concern, but an outcry goes further: it is the loud, emotional cry of many people at once, a wave of anger that erupts on its own rather than an event anyone organizes or schedules.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — ob-: against, in the way of

Root — ject: to throw (Latin jacere)

Suffix — -ion: act or process of

Put it together: Objection combines ob- (against) with ject (to throw) and -ion (the act of), so it literally means 'the act of throwing something against.' When you raise an objection, you throw your disagreement into the path of a proposal.

Use the root in a new word: trajectory: The physics class plotted the trajectory of the model rocket before launch.

Root Check

Word Choice

Formal / procedural

Common collocations: raise an objection, file an objection, overrule an objection. An objection is one specific, often formal act of opposing something, while dissent is broader, ongoing disagreement with an official position; you raise an objection to a single clause, but you dissent from the whole ruling.
